steps.body: **Parallel lines** stay exactly the same distance apart, forever — no matter how far you extend them, they never touch. Railroad tracks are the classic example: the two rails never get closer or farther apart, and never cross.
Construct parallel lines and test what rotation and translation change.

widget.prompt: Make the active blue line parallel to the dark line. Move BOTH controls so you can see that translation changes position but not direction.
widget.successFeedback: Parallel: same direction, constant distance, and no intersection even when extended.
widget.angleFeedback: The lines still have different directions. Match their angles so the gap stays constant.
widget.distanceFeedback: Use both rotation and translation. Parallel lines need the same direction and a nonzero gap.

predict.prompt: Two lines slanting by exactly the SAME amount — will they ever meet?

options.label: Only off the edge of the paper

predict.reveal: Equal slant means the gap between them never changes — extend them across the universe and they stay strangers. That's what parallel promises.

cml.actionGoal: Construct parallel lines while separating rotation from translation.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Translate after reaching the target relation. Which invariant survives, and which measurements change?

explanation.prompt: What changes when you translate instead of rotate?

options.label: Position changes while direction stays fixed.
options.feedback: Exactly — that separates translation from rotation.

options.label: Direction must change too.
options.feedback: Direction changes only when the line rotates.

explanationVariants: Parallel lines never cross, no matter how far they're extended — that's the entire test.
Same distance apart forever means they never meet.

widget.prompt: Two lines are the same distance apart everywhere and, when extended forever, never touch. What are they?

options.label: Parallel lines
options.feedback: Constant distance and never touching — the exact definition of parallel.

options.label: Perpendicular lines
options.feedback: Perpendicular lines CROSS at a right angle — these lines never cross at all. They're parallel.

options.label: Intersecting lines
options.feedback: Intersecting lines meet at a point. Lines that never touch are parallel.

options.label: Rays
options.feedback: A ray is about endpoints and direction, not about a relationship between two lines. Two lines that never meet are parallel.

steps.body: Diagrams mark parallel lines with matching arrow symbols — a single arrowhead (›) on each line in one parallel pair, double arrowheads (››) on a different pair. The matching arrows tell you which lines belong together.

explanationVariants: Lines marked with the same arrow symbol are parallel to each other.
Matching marks signal a matching relationship.

widget.prompt: In a diagram, line P and line R both have a single arrowhead mark; line Q has a double arrowhead mark. Which lines are parallel to each other?

options.label: P and R
options.feedback: Matching single-arrowhead marks mean P and R are parallel to each other.

options.label: P and Q
options.feedback: P and Q have DIFFERENT marks (single vs. double) — they're not marked as a parallel pair. P and R share the same mark.

options.label: Q and R
options.feedback: Q and R have different marks too. The matching pair is P and R, both with single arrowheads.

options.label: All three lines
options.feedback: Only lines with the SAME mark are parallel to each other. P and R match; Q is marked differently.

widget.prompt: Sort each example: parallel, or not?

items.label: Two opposite sides of a rectangular door
items.feedback: A rectangle's opposite sides stay the same distance apart — parallel.

items.label: The two edges of an open pair of scissors
items.feedback: The blades meet at the pivot — not parallel.

items.label: The rungs of a ladder
items.feedback: Each rung stays parallel to the others.

items.label: The letter X
items.feedback: The two strokes of an X cross in the middle — not parallel.

widget.missFeedback: Ask whether the two lines would ever touch if stretched out forever.
widget.successFeedback: Door edges and ladder rungs stay apart forever; scissor blades and the letter X both cross.

explanationVariants: Lines that are gradually getting closer together would eventually meet — that rules out parallel.
Parallel requires a CONSTANT distance, not just a similar direction.

widget.prompt: Two lines point in almost the same direction, but they're slowly getting closer together. Are they parallel?

options.label: They aren't — getting closer means they'll eventually meet
options.feedback: Parallel lines keep a CONSTANT distance forever. Slowly closing the gap means they'll eventually touch — not parallel.

options.label: Yes — they point in almost the same direction
options.feedback: Almost the same direction isn't the test — constant distance is. Since the gap is shrinking, they aren't parallel.

options.label: Yes — as long as they haven't touched yet
options.feedback: Not yet touching isn't the same as never touching. If the gap keeps shrinking, they eventually will.

options.label: Impossible to know without seeing them cross
options.feedback: The description already tells you: a shrinking gap means they aren't staying the same distance apart. Not parallel.

hints: Painted parking-space lines are meant to stay evenly spaced.
Check whether each pair stays the same distance apart.
A properly painted lot has every space line parallel to its neighbors.
explanationVariants: Properly painted parking lines stay the same distance apart along their whole length — parallel.
Even spacing everywhere is exactly the parallel test.

widget.prompt: A parking lot has painted lines dividing it into equal-width spaces, each line staying the same distance from its neighbors along its whole length. Are neighboring lines parallel?

options.label: Yes — they stay the same distance apart everywhere
options.feedback: Constant spacing along the whole length is exactly the definition of parallel.

options.label: No — parking lines are too short to be parallel
options.feedback: Length doesn't disqualify a pair from being parallel — constant distance does, and that's exactly what's described here.

options.label: Only if the parking lot is perfectly square
options.feedback: The lot's overall shape doesn't matter — what matters is whether the LINES themselves keep a constant distance apart, which they do here.

options.label: Can't tell without measuring every point
options.feedback: The description already confirms constant spacing along the whole length — that's sufficient to call them parallel.

takeaways: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart forever and never cross.
Matching arrow marks in a diagram show which lines are parallel to each other.
A shrinking gap between two lines means they aren't parallel — they'll eventually meet.
steps.teaser: next: lines that cross at exactly the right angle.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Parallel lines never cross, no matter how far they extend.** Picture two straight fence lines running side by side, always the same distance apart — that's the whole idea.

explanationVariants: Two fence lines always the same distance apart never cross — parallel.

widget.prompt: Two fence lines run side by side, always the same distance apart. Are they parallel?

options.label: Yes
options.feedback: Constant distance apart, never crossing — parallel.

options.label: Only if they're very long
options.feedback: Length isn't the test — constant distance is, and that's true here regardless of length.

options.label: Can't tell
options.feedback: The description already gives the answer: always the same distance apart means parallel.
